subject: literature
notes: Premchand (1880–1936) is one of the most celebrated writers of modern Hindi and Urdu fiction.
He was born Dhanpat Rai and first published his stories in Urdu under the name Nawab Rai.
In 1908, he published Soz-e-Watan, a collection of patriotic Urdu stories.
British colonial authorities banned the collection, and copies of it were burned.
Afterward, he began publishing under the new pen name Premchand.
His later works, such as the novel Godaan (1936), portray the hardships of village life.
stem: The student wants to explain how the writer came to use the name Premchand, including the name he had published under before. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Born Dhanpat Rai, the writer now celebrated as Premchand first published his stories in Urdu under the name Nawab Rai.
choices.B: Premchand, born Dhanpat Rai, became one of the most celebrated writers of Hindi and Urdu fiction, known for works such as Godaan.
choices.C: After British authorities banned and burned Soz-e-Watan, a 1908 collection of patriotic Urdu stories, its author's works were published under a new name.
choices.D: Once British authorities banned Soz-e-Watan, the patriotic stories he had published as Nawab Rai, the writer adopted the pen name Premchand.

explanation.why: The goal has two parts: the name he used before and the reason he came to use "Premchand." The notes connect them: the stories he had published as Nawab Rai were banned, and afterward he adopted the new pen name.
explanation.A: Incorrect. It gives his earlier pen name but does not explain why he changed it.
explanation.B: Incorrect. It gives his birth name and later fame, not how he came to use the name Premchand.
explanation.C: Incorrect. It explains the cause of the change but never says what the old or the new name was. This is the most attractive near miss because it tells the key event in detail.
explanation.D: Correct. It names the earlier pen name (Nawab Rai), the event that led to the change (the ban on Soz-e-Watan), and the new name.
